angle: Why a descending Falcon 9 booster must burn fuel to land safely.

beats.text: When a rocket booster falls back to Earth, gravity pulls it down at extreme speeds. To slow it down, an external force must act in the opposite direction of its motion.
A rocket creates this braking force by expelling onboard mass. Chemical combustion heats gases that expand and shoot out of the nozzle, pushing the vehicle in the opposite direction.
During descent, the Falcon 9 first-stage restarts engines for an entry burn to begin slowing down, while grid fins aerodynamically steer its descent.
Finally, a landing engine ignition fires. This downward exhaust provides the critical upward thrust that halts the booster's downward speed, achieving a soft vertical landing.

hook: Why does a reusable rocket need to burn fuel when it is already falling back to Earth?
